planting.note: Set nursery-grown divisions into a wet, acidic peat-and-sand bog mix in full sun in spring, and keep the pot standing in pure rain or distilled water year-round; this Gulf Coast native tolerates a milder, longer growing season than its northern relative Sarracenia purpurea.

directions: Gulf purple pitcher plant forms a low, sprawling rosette of squat, heavily veined pitchers that lie close to the ground rather than standing upright, luring ants and other crawling insects into the hooded tube where downward-pointing hairs and a pool of digestive fluid prevent escape. Native to wet longleaf pine savannas and seepage bogs along the Florida Panhandle and Gulf Coast, it was long treated as a form of Sarracenia purpurea before being recognized as its own species, and it tolerates the long, mild, humid growing season of the Deep South better than its northern relative. Grow it in full sun in a permanently saturated, nutrient-poor peat-and-sand bog mix, watering only with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water since dissolved minerals and fertilizer will kill the roots. Divide congested clumps in early spring and allow the foliage to die back naturally through a mild winter rest.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

common_name: Mountain Sweet Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia Rubra Subsp. Jonesii)

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring into a wet, acidic peat-sand bog mix and keep standing in pure rain or distilled water; unlike Gulf Coast Sarracenia, this Blue Ridge mountain endemic prefers a cooler, partly shaded seep site and benefits from a protective winter mulch of pine straw or sphagnum.

directions: Mountain sweet pitcher plant produces slender, upright, trumpet-shaped pitchers with a narrow hood and maroon venation over bright green, distinctly smaller and more delicate than the pitchers of typical Gulf Coast Sarracenia rubra. It survives only in a handful of high-elevation seepage bogs in the Blue Ridge Mountains of the Carolinas, so nursery-propagated plants should always be sourced from cultivated stock rather than the wild, where the species is federally endangered. Because it comes from cooler mountain seeps rather than the warm coastal plain, it appreciates a shadier, cooler bog site than lowland Sarracenia and benefits from a heavy winter mulch in colder parts of its range. Keep the bog medium of peat and sand permanently wet with pure rain or distilled water, and give it several hours of direct sun daily for the best pitcher color.

common_name: Tarnok Pitcher Plant (Continuous-Blooming White-Top Sarracenia Cultivar)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in spring and set into pure long-fiber sphagnum moss or a 1:1 peat-perlite mix, keeping the pot standing in rain or distilled water at all times; this registered cultivar produces pitchers over a much longer season than typical Sarracenia leucophylla.

directions: 'Tarnok' is a compact, heavy-blooming selection of the white-topped pitcher plant, prized for its unusual double, pinecone-like red flowers and for pitchers that emerge continuously from mid-spring through early fall rather than only in late summer like typical Sarracenia leucophylla. Its tall, narrow pitchers still show the parent species' brilliant white, red-veined upper hood, but the plant grows into a denser, more floriferous clump than wild-type forms. Grow it exactly as you would the species: full sun, a permanently wet, nutrient-poor peat-sand or sphagnum bog medium, and irrigation with only rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water, since minerals and fertilizer damage the fine root system. Divide the spreading rhizome in early spring and allow a natural winter dormancy with reduced light and moisture for long-term vigor.

common_name: Leah Wilkerson Pitcher Plant (Giant White-and-Yellow Sarracenia Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in spring and plant into pure long-fiber sphagnum moss or a 1:1 peat-perlite mix, keeping the pot standing in rain or distilled water at all times; give this vigorous natural hybrid extra spacing since its pitchers can grow taller than two feet.

directions: 'Leah Wilkerson' is a spectacular natural hybrid between the white-topped pitcher plant and the yellow trumpet pitcher plant, discovered in a Florida panhandle bog and prized in cultivation for producing some of the tallest pitchers of any Sarracenia, occasionally exceeding two feet with heavy venation and a glowing white, pink-rimmed hood. It combines the vigor and easy growth of both parent species, forming large, dramatic clumps within a few growing seasons when given adequate space. As with other Sarracenia, plant it in full sun in a permanently saturated, nutrient-poor peat-and-sand or sphagnum medium, watering only with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water. Divide congested rhizomes in early spring and let the plant experience a natural winter dormancy with reduced watering and light for continued strong growth.

planting.note: Set transplants into a lean mix of peat with added sand and crushed limestone or dolomite to mimic its native calcareous fen habitat, keeping it constantly moist with rain or distilled water; slender-leaved sundew needs roughly nine months of cold winter dormancy each year and declines in climates too mild to provide it.

directions: Slender-leaved sundew forms a low tuft of narrow, upright, grass-like leaves edged in reddish glandular tentacles that trap and slowly digest small insects, and it is unusual among sundews for growing naturally in calcium-rich marl fens of the Great Lakes region and Canadian Maritimes rather than the acidic bogs most Drosera prefer. It is also one of the most demanding sundews in cultivation, requiring roughly nine months of true winter dormancy each year and tending to decline in mild climates where it cannot fully rest. Grow it outdoors in a lean, constantly moist mix such as peat with added sand, limestone chips, or dolomite to mimic its native mineral-rich fen habitat, using rain or distilled water rather than the purely acidic bog blends formulated for typical sundews. Give it full sun and a genuine cold winter with reduced moisture to allow the plant to form its protective winter bud.

planting.note: Set transplants into a 1:1 mix of peat and sand or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss kept constantly wet with rain or distilled water; great sundew needs a genuine freezing winter dormancy and performs poorly in mild climates without an artificial cold rest.

directions: Great sundew is a robust, cold-hardy relative of the round-leaved sundew, forming upright, narrow, spoon-shaped leaves densely fringed with sticky red tentacles that trap insects across the circumboreal bogs and fens where it grows from Alaska and Canada south into the northern United States. It requires a genuine freezing winter dormancy, dying back to a small resting bud that resists ice before resuming growth in spring, and it struggles in warm climates without an artificial cold rest such as refrigeration. Grow it in a constantly wet, nutrient-poor mix of peat and sand or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss in full sun, watering only with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water since minerals and fertilizer will damage its roots. Allow the foliage to die back naturally each fall and avoid forcing continued growth once dormancy begins.

planting.note: Set transplants into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss kept in a tray of rain or distilled water; this all-green, white-flowered form is grown exactly like the species and needs no winter dormancy.

directions: The 'Alba' cultivar of Cape sundew is an all-green form lacking the reddish pigment of the typical Cape sundew, with pale green, dew-covered, strap-shaped leaves and white rather than pink flowers, otherwise sharing the same easygoing nature that makes this species a favorite beginner carnivorous plant. Sticky glandular tentacles along the leaf margins curl slowly around trapped insects to supply nutrients the poor native fynbos soil of South Africa's Cape region cannot provide. Grow it in bright light in a constantly moist mix of peat and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss, watering the tray only with rain or distilled water, since tap water minerals and fertilizer will harm the plant. Unlike cold-hardy sundews, it needs no winter dormancy and can be grown as a year-round houseplant in a sunny window or under grow lights in climates outside zones 9-11.

planting.note: Set small divisions or plugs directly into pure living or dead sphagnum moss kept constantly moist but not waterlogged, watering only with rain or distilled water; this subarctic species needs a long, genuine cold dormancy and cool, humid summers to persist.

directions: Hairy butterwort is one of the smallest and most cold-adapted butterworts, forming a tiny rosette of sticky, glue-covered leaves barely an inch across that traps and digests gnats and other minute insects on the surface of sphagnum hummocks in subarctic bogs and muskegs of Canada, Alaska, and the far northern United States. It is considerably more difficult to keep alive in cultivation than the popular Mexican butterworts, requiring consistently cool, humid conditions and a genuine, often lengthy, cold dormancy to survive from year to year. Grow it in pure living or dead sphagnum moss kept constantly moist but never waterlogged, in bright but not scorching light, and irrigate only with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water, since it is extremely sensitive to dissolved minerals. Because of its minute size and exacting needs it is best suited to a dedicated cold bog terrarium or an outdoor peat bog in far northern gardens rather than a typical windowsill collection.
sources: Government of Northwest Territories Species Search
